Each name in the list is a reminder that God knows and values each of us.

55.epoque: This passage is set during the return of the Jewish exiles from Babylon to Jerusalem, after the deportation, around the end of the 6th century B.C.

56.epoque: This verse is set in the context of the return of the Jewish exiles from Babylon to Jerusalem, after the deportation that took place in the 6th century B.C.

56.commentaire: The return of the exiles is a powerful symbol of redemption and restoration. Just as these families left Babylon to return to Jerusalem, we are called to leave our own 'Babylons' – places of despair and distance from God – to embrace the life that God has planned for us. This passage encourages us to engage in our faith community and actively participate in building God's kingdom on earth.

mots.sens: The name 'Schephathia' means 'Yahweh has judged' or 'the judgment of God'. This name evokes divine justice and God's role as judge. In the context of the return of the exiles, it reminds us that God is sovereign over events and that He restores His people according to His justice. This underscores God's faithfulness to those who return to Him.

The term 'Hatthil' is less known, but it could be interpreted as 'the strong one' or 'the friend'. This name can symbolize strength and solidarity within the community. Spiritually, it reminds us of the importance of unity and mutual support in faith, especially during times of return and rebuilding.

The name 'Pokéreth-Hatsebaïm' could be translated as 'the one who is the guardian of the gardens'. This term evokes protection and care for the land, an essential aspect in the context of the return to Jerusalem. Theologically, it can symbolize God's care for His people and His desire to see the land flourish and prosper under His blessing.

The word 'Ami' means 'my people' and emphasizes the collective identity of the descendants of Israel. It reminds us of the unbreakable bond between God and His people, as well as belonging to a community of faith. In this verse, it reinforces the idea that even in exile, God's people remain united and are called to gather for divine service.

This encourages us to recognize our own place in the faith community and to actively contribute to God's mission in the world.

59.epoque: This passage is set during the time of the Jewish return from exile to Jerusalem, after the deportation to Babylon, around 538 B.C.

65.epoque: This passage takes place after the Babylonian exile, at a time when the Israelites are returning to Jerusalem to rebuild the temple and restore their national and religious identity.

66.epoque: This verse takes place after the return of the Jewish exiles from Babylon, under the reign of Cyrus, around 538 B.C., a period marked by the rebuilding of Jerusalem and the temple.

Just as these animals helped the people regain their land, we too are called to be instruments of God to carry the Gospel and support others in their spiritual journey. May we recognize and appreciate the resources God provides us to fulfill His will.

mots.sens: The word 'beit' means 'house' and is often used to refer not only to a physical structure but also to a place of meeting with God. In the biblical context, it evokes the idea of divine presence and the community of believers. The house of God is a symbol of the relationship between God and His people, highlighting the importance of devotion and worship.

The term 'min'cha' refers to an offering, often a grain or food offering, presented to God. This notion of voluntary offering emphasizes the act of devotion and gratitude towards God. Spiritually, it represents the acknowledgment of God's sovereignty over our possessions and the willingness to contribute to His work.

The word 'nasi' designates a chief or leader, often in reference to a recognized authority among the people. In this verse, it underscores the importance of spiritual leadership in the process of restoring worship. The actions of family leaders inspire the community to engage in the reconstruction of God's house, thus showing the crucial role of leadership in faith.

The term 'Yerushalayim' refers to Jerusalem, the holy city and spiritual center of the people of Israel. It is seen as the place where God chooses to dwell among His people. Jerusalem symbolizes the hope of restoration and redemption, and its restoration is essential for the spiritual life of the nation.

68.epoque: This passage takes place after the Babylonian exile, when the Israelites return to Jerusalem to rebuild their city and temple, marking a significant turning point in their spiritual and national history.
68.passage: Ezra 2 describes the return of the exiles and their commitment to restore the worship of God. This verse highlights the importance of voluntary offerings for the reconstruction of God's house, symbolizing the devotion of the people.
68.culture: In Israelite culture, offerings were an act of devotion and acknowledgment towards God. They were often seen as a means of maintaining a close relationship with the divine and actively participating in community life.
68.interpretation: This verse emphasizes the importance of generosity and personal commitment in serving God. The voluntary offerings of family leaders illustrate a collective response to God's call to restore His temple, symbolizing a new era of devotion and faithfulness.
68.commentaire: This passage reminds us that spiritual restoration requires active commitment from everyone. By offering voluntarily, the family leaders show that worship and the house of God are priorities. This invites us to reflect on our own commitment to God's work and how we can contribute to His house, both materially and spiritually.

mots.sens: The word 'dariq' designates a unit of monetary measure, often translated as 'drachma'. This term is related to wealth and abundance, and it underscores the value of gold in the economic context of the time. Spiritually, it symbolizes the generosity and commitment of believers to contribute to God's work.

The word 'minah' refers to a unit of weight for money, often used in commercial transactions. This evokes the idea of value and sacrifice, indicating that the gifts were significant. Theologically, it reminds us that every contribution, regardless of its size, is precious in God's eyes.

The word 'ketonet' means 'tunic' and refers to a specific garment worn by the priests. These tunics symbolize holiness and service in worship. Spiritually, they represent the importance of preparation and consecration for serving God.

69.epoque: This passage takes place during the return of the Jewish exiles from Babylon to Jerusalem, after the fall of Babylon in 539 B.C., marking a turning point in the history of the people of Israel.
69.passage: Ezra 2 describes the census of the exiles returning to Jerusalem and the gifts they bring for the reconstruction of the temple, highlighting community commitment and faith in spiritual restoration.
69.culture: In the Jewish culture of the time, gifts to the temple were seen as acts of devotion and responsibility towards God. This reflects a deep understanding of the relationship between material prosperity and spiritual service.
69.interpretation: This verse shows that contributing to the treasury of God's work is an act of faith and solidarity. Every gift, whether in gold, silver, or clothing, is a testimony of the believers' commitment to the divine mission.
69.commentaire: The gifts of the exiles to the treasury of the work are a powerful example of how we can participate in God's work. It reminds us that our generosity, in whatever form, plays an essential role in building God's kingdom on earth. Let us be encouraged to give according to our means, knowing that every contribution has eternal value.

mots.sens: This term designates a priest, a person consecrated to the service of God, particularly in worship and sacrifices. The root of this word evokes the idea of mediation between God and the people, underscoring the importance of the priestly role in the relationship with the divine. In this verse, it reminds us that serving God must be at the center of the communal life of Israel.

The term refers to the Levites, members of the tribe of Levi, who were responsible for sacred tasks in the tabernacle and later in the temple. Their role was crucial for worship and adoration, as they assisted the priests and took care of the practical aspects of divine service. Spiritually, they symbolize devotion and service to God within the community.

This word designates the Nethinim, servants dedicated to the service of the temple, often considered assistants to the Levites. Their presence underscores the importance of every member of the community in worship and service to God. Theologically, they represent the diversity of roles in the body of Christ, each having a valuable function within the community.

This term means 'city' and evokes a place of community life and social organization. In the biblical context, cities were centers of worship, commerce, and social life. Spiritually, this reminds us that God desires His people to live in community, sharing faith and mutual support in an organized setting.

70.epoque: This passage takes place after the return of the exiles from Babylon, at a time when Israel seeks to rebuild its national and spiritual identity.
70.passage: In Ezra 2, the people of God are in the process of reestablishing themselves in their promised land after years of exile, and this verse highlights the importance of community organization for worship and daily life.
70.culture: At this time, the social structure of Israel was closely tied to religion, with clearly defined roles for priests, Levites, and other members of the people, each having a function in worship.
70.interpretation: This verse shows that every group, from priests to Nethinim, has an essential role in the spiritual life of Israel. It underscores the importance of community in serving God and the necessity of organization to live out faith.
70.commentaire: This passage reminds us that the Christian life is lived in community, where every member has a role to play in serving God. By establishing ourselves in our 'cities', that is, in our communities, we are called to actively live out our faith, supporting one another in our walk with Christ.
